articles.title: Grocers issue warning over Mamdani’s taxpayer-backed stores: 'We're going to go after' them
articles.summary: Frank Garcia's coalition threatens to sue any operator joining Zohran Mamdani's NYC government-owned grocery store program in new legal fight.
articles.body: Private operators looking to run New York City’s planned government-owned grocery stores are being put on notice: Join Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s program, and grocers fighting the plan say they could face you in court. "We’re going to go after any operator that’s in there," Frank Garcia, who is leading a coalition of immigrant-owned grocers challenging the city’s plan, told Fox News Digital in an interview Monday. "We’re hoping that no one puts the RFP." NEW YORK CITY IMMIGRANT BUSINESS OWNERS ARE PLANNING TO SUE MAMDANI OVER TAXPAYER-FUNDED SUPERMARKETS Garcia, chairman of the Multicultural Business Coalition, was referring to New York City’s request for proposals seeking private operators to run the five taxpayer-backed grocery stores Mamdani has proposed. Under the program, selected operators would receive city-backed space while agreeing to sell a core basket of groceries at prices 30% below typical New York City retail prices. The Multicultural Business Coalition filed two lawsuits against the city Monday, arguing the taxpayer-backed stores would unfairly compete with minority- and immigrant-owned businesses already operating on thin margins. Garcia said the coalition now intends to extend that legal fight to private companies that sign on to operate the stores. GROCERY BOSS WARNS MAMDANI'S CITY-RUN STORES PIT GOVERNMENT AGAINST 'ITS OWN CITIZENS' The threat comes as the city moves from pitching the concept to trying to find companies willing to run it. The New York City Economic Development Corporation formally opened the operator RFP in July and is seeking up to five companies to operate the stores. Proposals are due Oct. 16. Mamdani has said the five stores, one in each borough, are expected to open by 2029. The administration says shoppers would receive a fixed 30% discount on a basket that includes fresh produce, meat and seafood, along with staples such as milk, bread, cheese, pasta, rice and beans. Existing grocers, however, argue they would be forced to compete against stores insulated from costs they have to shoulder themselves, particularly rent. Mamdani has pushed back on claims that the municipal stores would put neighborhood bodegas out of business, pointing out that the city-backed locations would not sell products such as cigarettes, alcohol, lottery tickets or hot foods — revenue streams that can help sustain smaller neighborhood stores. The mayor has also pointed to public-market models such as Essex Market as evidence that subsidized markets and private businesses can coexist. "I’m confident in both the legality of this – that it will stand up in court – and the importance of delivering it," Mamdani said in a news conference on Monday. Asked what he was doing for bodega owners who worry about losing business, Mamdani said: "What we can do is continue with our approach citywide of looking for ways to cut costs and cut the regulations that so many bodegueros, as well as grocery store owners, have to jump through in order to do their work. What we have already found through our OPEN Task Force is already the identification of more than 50 potential changes that target things from the current necessity of having two different licenses to sell hot food and cold, dairy frozen dessert. As well as the kinds of things that make it harder for bodegas to both sell items outside of the store and inside of the store." The mayor’s office declined to comment on Garcia’s claim that his coalition sought a meeting with Mamdani and did not respond to his threat of litigation against participating operators. Garcia said his coalition sought a meeting with Mamdani before going to court but was rebuffed, alleging the mayor instead met with a group of Dominican business owners while leaving out other immigrant and minority-owned businesses that could be affected by the plan. "He’s putting our minority businesses against minority businesses," Garcia said. Garcia repeatedly invoked the immigrant history of New York’s bodegas, describing businesses that have passed through generations of Puerto Rican, Dominican, Mexican and other immigrant entrepreneurs. His coalition, he said, represents a broader cross-section of those businesses, including Latino, Korean and Arab store owners. City officials have also wrestled with how to support existing grocers that fear they could lose business to the taxpayer-backed stores. Waverly Neer, a senior vice president at the New York City Economic Development Corporation (NYCEDC) who leads the NYC Groceries initiative, recently said the agency was considering grants and other incentives that could accompany the municipal stores and support independent businesses in surrounding neighborhoods. NYCEDC later said grants were not currently under consideration but that the agency was exploring other forms of assistance, including potential tax abatements, incentives and zoning benefits through existing city programs. MAMDANI’S CITY GROCERY PLAN COULD LEAVE TAXPAYERS PAYING FOR EVERY BANANA Garcia argues the city should put more of its resources behind businesses that already exist. He said some immigrant-owned bodegas in his coalition have struggled to access affordable capital and turned instead to private lenders charging steep rates. "A lot of these bodegas are paying 35% loans right now to predator lenders," Garcia said. His criticism was not reserved for Mamdani or Democrats. Garcia said Republicans have also "hurt us," pointing to federal restrictions affecting access to Small Business Administration-backed loans for green-card holders, while arguing elected officials across the political spectrum have failed immigrant entrepreneurs seeking affordable capital. But Garcia saved his sharpest political criticism for Mamdani’s democratic socialist allies, saying the coalition intends to mobilize against the movement as its fight over the grocery stores expands. "We are creating a path to go after the DSA," Garcia said. Garcia insisted the coalition is not simply asking the city to abandon its effort to bring down grocery prices. Instead of creating new city-backed competitors, he said grocers have proposed forming a buying group that would allow independent stores to purchase goods directly from manufacturers, cutting out middlemen and lowering participating stores’ costs. "We have other solutions," Garcia said. "Work with us to create that." SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Garcia said the coalition believes the city could use existing minority-business programs and its purchasing power to expand the model, allowing private neighborhood stores to lower prices without forcing them to compete against rent-free municipal stores. articles.title: JONATHAN TURLEY:  Abdul El-Sayed’s wealth-tax fantasy could wreck the Michigan economy
articles.summary: Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed frames extreme wealth as an existential threat, but critics warn his tax plan could trigger an exodus of top earners from Michigan.
articles.body: Dr. Abdul El-Sayed is tackling a new national crisis: the excess of money held by some tragically wealthy citizens. In his interview this week with Fox News’ Jesse Watters, the Michigan Democratic Senate candidate not only reaffirmed his call for a wealth tax but suggested that wealthy people really do not have much use for money that would be better left to the public. El-Sayed needs money. A lot of money. He has called for massive new programs to fund Medicare-for-All, reparations, roads and other programs promised to Michigan voters. He is only the latest Democratic leader to support a wealth tax, which would, in my opinion, be unconstitutional at the federal level and disastrous at the state level. ABDUL EL-SAYED GRILLED ON PAST STATEMENTS ON SHARIA LAW AND WHITE SUPREMACY, TAXING THE RICH Earlier in the week, El-Sayed expressed full support for a wealth tax, including on non-billionaires. He declared on a podcast: "I also think we got to start taxing wealth for people who now have over $100 million. I mean at that point like what are gonna even do with more money?" Figures such as Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., have also called for a wealth tax on millionaires, not just billionaires. As some of us predicted, the use of billionaires was simply a strategic and political framing. Once politicians succeed in opening up this untapped wealth to taxation, they will gradually work down the tax rolls as they acquire a windfall in new revenue. PROGRESSIVES WANT TO TAX BILLIONAIRES FIRST, AND YOU'RE NEXT ON THE LIST I discuss the tax in my book, "Rage and the Republic," as an example of the "eat-the-rich" politics used by demagogues from ancient Athens to the French Revolution. Politicians seek to divide a population into "haves" and "have-nots" with the promise that citizens can have it all. Much of what El-Sayed said is ripped from the pages of figures such as Huey Long and his "Share Our Wealth" campaigns of the 1930s. In his Fox News interview, El-Sayed reaffirmed his call for a wealth tax, adding: "The question ultimately is, ‘Do you want to drive on good roads, or would you rather have a billionaire make a second billion?’ That’s what Mike Rogers wants. That’s why Donald Trump wants. Apparently, that’s what you want. I think the people in Michigan want something different." While El-Sayed and his wife reported $686,069 in income in 2025, they would not be subject to the wealth tax. It would apply to those with $100 million or more in property and other forms of wealth. EL-SAYED IN THE HOT SEAT FOR ANOTHER FOREIGN RENTAL PROPERTY, NEARLY $300K IN ADDITIONAL INCOME El-Sayed appears to conflate or confuse wealth taxes and income taxes in the interview. He told Watters, "If we tax you at 7%, you’re still going to make what? A cool $30 million off your billion dollars? I think that’s OK, they’re going to be OK, Jesse." El-Sayed did not explain his assumptions. He may have been assuming that a $1 billion fortune generates a 10% annual return: $100 million in gains, less a hypothetical 7% wealth tax of $70 million, leaving $30 million. Whether such a return, tax rate and tax base are realistic is a separate question. As Michigan struggles to secure new businesses and jobs, El-Sayed is embracing the same policies that would decapitate the top of its tax base. There is a great difference between a wealth tax and an income tax. The wealthy have already paid taxes on much of their wealth. Indeed, they pay income taxes when the money is earned and pay taxes on any profits from that money when it is invested in stock or property. A wealth tax is an additional tax on all that you own, from homes to boats to art. At a 7% tax on wealth for those worth $100,000,000, the wealthy would pay an additional $7,000,000 every year in Michigan beyond their income taxes. SIX DIFFERENT WAYS THAT PROVE THE WEALTHY PAY A LOT MORE THAN THEIR ‘FAIR SHARE’ If a government imposed a 7% annual tax on $100 million in net wealth, the annual liability would be $7 million—though El-Sayed has not released a detailed proposal establishing that rate or threshold. In Michigan, they would also face the state income tax of 4.25% and a 6% corporate tax on their businesses. If the wealth tax is added to an income tax, that would be in addition to the 37% top federal income tax rate. Again, the wealth tax would continue to apply each year to what an individual owns in the form of cars, homes and other property, regardless of whether income declines. AOC TRIPLES DOWN, CLAIMS AMERICAN REVOLUTION WAS AGAINST 'THE BILLIONAIRES OF THEIR TIME' Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., drove this point home when she ran for president in 2020, taunting the wealthy that she was coming for "your Rembrandts, your stock portfolio, your diamonds and your yachts." While some states are actively considering a wealth tax, many of us view it as unconstitutional under the federal system. The federal government secured the right to tax individuals in 1913, but the 16th Amendment only approved income taxes. DAVID MARCUS: HOW DEMOCRATS SNEAKED IN REPARATIONS, AND HOW THEY'LL PROTECT THEM This is why many of these same politicians are promising a hostile takeover of the Supreme Court by either eliminating the Court or packing it with an instant liberal majority. Once packed, the Court could greenlight a variety of unconstitutional measures. Years ago, Harvard professor Michael Klarman laid out a radical agenda to change the system to guarantee Republicans will never win another election. However, he warned that "the Supreme Court could strike down everything I just described." Therefore, the Court must be packed in advance to allow these changes to occur. DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS HAVE LOTS OF IDEAS, BUT HOW ARE WE SUPPOSED TO PAY FOR THEM? Even if states like Michigan are allowed to do this, it will result in the same exodus that is currently unfolding in California, where possibly trillions of dollars in jobs and revenue have already been lost due to the mere threat of wealth taxes. That is why figures like Khanna and Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., are calling for a national wealth tax, leaving the wealthy nowhere to go but out of the country. This is precisely what socialist governments like France under François Mitterrand attempted in the last century, with disastrous results that tanked the economy and forced a rapid retreat from such policies. THE ONLY MAP YOU NEED TO SEE AS CALIFORNIA'S BILLIONAIRE TAX FIGHT HEATS UP As Michigan struggles to secure new businesses and jobs, El-Sayed is embracing the same policies that would decapitate the top of its tax base. While repeating the mantra that the wealthy are "not paying their fair share," the top 10% pays more in federal income taxes than the bottom 90% combined. In 2023, the top 1% paid an estimated 38.4% of all federal individual income taxes. El-Sayed has proven himself a gifted politician. He juxtaposes concrete benefits like new roads with the image of unused wealth among top earners. The fact is that Michigan will have fewer roads if it chases away top earners with their businesses and jobs. Like Long, who referred to "our wealth" being held by the rich, El-Sayed portrays the property of the wealthy as rightfully belonging to the people, promising that if we "put a tax on wealth it would return a lot of that money back into public use." El-Sayed has perfected the "eat-the-rich" pitch by portraying the wealthy as virtual Scrooge McDucks who accumulate unused wealth as a type of vanity project. He has struck out at "people who have accumulated so much wealth that your money makes money." That is also called investments that power the economy—and when your "money makes money," it is taxed as income. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Nevertheless, El-Sayed is waging the same class war as other rising figures in the Democratic Party, denouncing "extreme wealth" as "an existential threat to our economy and our democracy and it demands a crisis-level response." The real crisis is unfolding as candidates like El-Sayed are promising trillions in new programs while promising to make the rich pay for them. As with Warren, their property is being portrayed as rightfully belonging to the public. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The problem is that both wealth and the wealthy are mobile, and few are likely to stick around for El-Sayed’s people’s paradise in Michigan. articles.title: AOC says ‘Woke 1 was crazy,’ but Democrats still owe voters an explanation
articles.summary: New York Democrat Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez's "Woke 1" label lets Democrats compartmentalize 2020 progressive politics without a reckoning.
articles.body: "Woke 1 was crazy." New York Democrat Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez recently borrowed the phrase from New York City Councilman Chi Ossé to describe the politics of 2020. "Woke 1" gives Democrats a convenient way to put ideas such as defunding the police and abolishing prisons in the past. That was then. This is now. There’s a psychological term for this kind of separation: compartmentalization. Consider how compartmentalization works in ordinary life. A married man can have a wife and children at home and a girlfriend on the side, keeping the two lives separate enough that he rarely confronts the contradiction. Compartmentalization allows us to separate conflicting parts of our lives rather than reconcile them. ALEXANDRIA OCASIO-CORTEZ SHRUGS OFF PAST 'DEFUND THE POLICE' COMMENTS, JOKING 'WOKE 1 WAS CRAZY' That appears to be what Democrats are trying to do with 2020. There is the Democratic Party of 2020, when progressive ideas that once sat outside the mainstream suddenly gained influence. Then there is the Democratic Party of 2026, talking about affordability, economic populism and winning back voters who recoiled from the cultural politics of the past several years. "Woke 1" puts a neat dividing line between them. Changing your mind requires confronting what you once believed. Compartmentalization doesn’t. Many political beliefs in 2020 became tests of character. They didn’t just say what you believed. They said what kind of person you were. If people you dismissed six years ago turned out to have a point, you have more to reconsider than a policy. Maybe you were too certain. Maybe you mistook disagreement for prejudice. MICHIGAN SENATE HOPEFUL ABDUL EL-SAYED FIRES BACK AT CNN CHOOSING TO 'FIXATE' ON 'DEFUND THE POLICE' COMMENTS Or you can call the whole thing Woke 1. Except 2020 didn’t simply happen to the Democratic Party. Politicians embraced ideas, activists pushed them, and institutions decided which arguments deserved a hearing and which could be dismissed. People who challenged the prevailing views sometimes paid a price for it. Calling all of this "Woke 1" makes those choices sound like the product of a strange moment everyone has since outgrown. AOC'S ATTEMPT TO DISMISS 'WOKE 1' AS 'CRAZY' DRAWS CRITICISM FROM LEFT-LEANING OUTLETS If Democrats now reject positions they embraced or tolerated in 2020, voters can reasonably expect an explanation. The key question is whether Democrats changed their minds or discovered that voters had. There is nothing shameful about changing your mind. Real change requires connecting what you believed then with what you believe now and acknowledging where you got it wrong. Without that reckoning, voters are left to wonder whether the beliefs changed or the incentives did. DNC’S 192-PAGE AUTOPSY SOUNDS LIKE BAD THERAPY. DEMOCRATS STILL HAVE A BIG PROBLEM Democrats can compartmentalize 2020. Voters don’t have to. A candidate may regard a six-year-old position as ancient history, but an opponent can revive it with an old interview, campaign questionnaire or social media post. "That was then" invites an obvious response: Yes, but that was you. DEMOCRATIC SENATE CANDIDATE CALLED FOR MASS RELEASE OF CRIMINALS DURING PRISON ABOLITION WEBINAR Democrats aren’t unique in doing this. Every political party finds ways to distance itself from positions that become inconvenient. But 2020 poses a particular problem because so many political beliefs became tied to moral identity. Giving up a position can feel like admitting something about yourself, not just admitting that a policy was wrong. If Democrats now reject positions they embraced or tolerated in 2020, voters can reasonably expect an explanation. The key question is whether Democrats changed their minds or discovered that voters had. There is a way out. Democrats could acknowledge that 2020 drew attention to genuine problems while also producing bad ideas. They could concede that some rhetoric went too far and that some people were treated unfairly for challenging the prevailing consensus. That doesn’t require abandoning concern about racism, police misconduct or inequality. It requires admitting that you can feel morally certain and still be wrong. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION The familiar Democratic argument is about whether the party should move left or toward the center. "Woke 1" raises a more interesting question: Before Democrats decide where they are going, can they explain what they now think about where they have been? CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Woke 1 was crazy" sounds like a confession. But it isn’t quite one. A confession names what you got wrong. Compartmentalization puts it somewhere you no longer have to look. CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM JONATHAN ALPERT

articles.title: GOP faces jam-packed September with funding, reconciliation on agenda
articles.summary: Republicans in both chambers are staring down a September sprint after returning from August recess, with a jam-packed legislative agenda and little time to clear their biggest remaining priorities before the midterm election crunch. At the top of the House’s list is passing a short-term stopgap spending measure — also known as a continuing resolution…
articles.body:
Republicans in both chambers are staring down a September sprint after returning from August recess, with a jam-packed legislative agenda and little time to clear their biggest remaining priorities before the midterm election crunch.

At the top of the House’s list is passing a short-term stopgap spending measure — also known as a continuing resolution (CR) — to avert a potential shutdown and keep the government funded past the Sept. 30 fiscal deadline.

What will likely be more of a headache for the GOP in both chambers is trying to push through a third reconciliation package that President Trump has been clamoring for.

The House passed a budget blueprint last month that outlined $73 billion in defense and intelligence funding, $12 billion for agriculture aid and $10 billion for a fund aimed at incentivizing states to adopt Trump-backed voting restrictions.

But a number of Republicans in the upper chamber railed against the House-passed budget resolution. Sen. Ron Johnson (R-Wis.), the Senate Budget Committee’s chair, released the GOP version of the budget resolution in early August, which the chamber didn’t take up before leaving for its recess.

In addition, the Senate ended up reaching a deal to postpone action on a college sports bill pushed by Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) after failing to agree on whether to hold votes to proceed to the bill. The Senate, however, did pass a bill to expand sanctions targeting Russia , which the House is expected to take up when the lower chamber returns from its recess.

The annual defense policy bill, the farm bill and a measure to reauthorize the nation’s foreign spy powers are also on the list of unfinished congressional business, though priorities will almost certainly slip until after the midterms.

The lower chamber returns next week, only to leave Washington again the week after, while the upper chamber isn’t slated to return until Sept. 14. That leaves Republicans in the House and Senate with roughly three weeks to work on their top priorities before leaving for another monthlong recess in October.

“There’s no question we have a packed September ahead of us, but that’s nothing new in Congress. There is a lot of important work that needs to get done, and funding the government responsibly will be a major priority when we return to Washington. I’m focused on working with my colleagues, being thoughtful about where we spend taxpayer dollars, and making sure we’re delivering for the people we represent. We have a full agenda ahead, and I’m confident we can make it a productive month,” Rep. Rich McCormick (R-Ga.) told The Hill in a statement.

But others are less hopeful that Republicans will achieve much in September.

“I’m not sure much gets done in September in Congress. The Senate left town before passing the reconciliation bill. That was the big thing that needed to be done, make sure that we replenish our munitions, and they abandoned town. I just don’t think much gets done before the election,” Rep. Andy Harris (R-Md.) told Fox News last week.

One area lawmakers are optimistic about is passing a CR and preventing a politically dangerous shutdown ahead of the midterms.

The House passed a CR last month that would fund the government at existing levels through Dec. 4. The Senate in early August easily passed its own version of a CR that would fund the government through Dec. 11, sending it to the House.

The Senate version of the CR also includes a provision to temporarily halt a rule from the White House budget office that would give political appointees in the executive branch more authority over dispersing federal grants — a provision that some Republicans in the lower chamber may not favor.

“We’ll have to see how that plays in the House,” House Majority Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.) said on Fox News earlier month about the Senate CR. “Again, the House has passed one completely clean through Dec. 4”

Still, the overwhelming margin of passage in the upper chamber — 90-6 — and the fact that the House passed its own CR early on has left little doubt that the Senate-passed measure could make it through the lower chamber.

Rep. Randy Fine (R-Fla.) told The Hill that he needs to look at the Senate CR “a little bit more closely to understand the differences. But my understanding is that the bills are not so far apart that we won’t be able to get to an answer.”

Asked about whether he was confident Republicans will get a CR across the finish line, Fine said, “I’m very confident about the CR because the Senate has passed one. So while they’re not the same, the fact that they have interest in doing it, and we have interest in doing it, makes me optimistic we’ll get something over the finish line.”

The budget reconciliation bill, meanwhile, faces a more daunting path.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.), Trump and conservatives in the upper chamber struck a deal to postpone action on a budget resolution until after recess. Johnson had noted then that some colleagues wanted more than $73 billion in defense funding.

Fiscal hawk conservatives in the Senate also demanded offsets in any reconciliation package, which the House-passed version does not have.

“There’s certainly concern in terms of the need for our military. When the finest among us are in harm’s way, is it really enough?” Johnson said earlier this month.

“The conclusion of the conference and then we had the discussion with the president, he agrees … just work diligently through August and September to do an actually better budget reconciliation bill,” the Senate’s Budget Committee chair continued.

Conservatives have been eyeing the third reconciliation bill as a vehicle to advance the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (SAVE America) Act, a long-standing conservative priority that would require providing proof of citizenship when registering to vote in federal elections and presenting photo identification when casting a ballot.

“I presume if it doesn’t happen in September, it might get revisited after the November election,” Fine said when asked about the timeline of a third reconciliation bill. “But it’s important to me to get it passed because we need to fund defense, and we need to get the SAVE America Act passed so our voters can see that we’re serious about securing our elections.”

He added, “I do wish we had offsets. However, if we have to pass it without offsets in order to get the SAVE America Act passed, that’s something I would support because the country will collapse because we no longer have faith in our elections before it will collapse under our debt.”

Republicans are also eyeing other priorities, including finalizing the annual defense policy bill known as the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA).

Senate Democrats defeated a motion to proceed to the $1.15 trillion annual defense authorization bill last month. They cited the resumption of the military conflict with Iran and Trump’s failure to ask Congress to authorize the war — which started on Feb. 28 — as a big reason behind their opposition to the NDAA.

Republicans in the upper chamber are also hoping to complete work on legislation that would impose harsher sanctions on Russia and the top five buyers of Russian oil, along with extending existing sanctions on Iran. The bill passed overwhelmingly in the Senate this month, and the House will likely take it up after recess.

Also on the table is legislation reauthorizing agricultural and food programs. While the House had passed a farm bill back in April, the Senate Agriculture Committee failed to advance the upper chamber’s version of the bill this month.

articles.title: Susan Collins tries to keep Trump off the ballot in Maine
articles.summary: During a campaign stop in South Carolina last week, President Trump urged Republicans to turn out and vote as if he were on the ballot. Sen. Susan Collins (R), fighting an uphill re-election battle in blue-leaning Maine, is sending the opposite signal, flexing her independent streak and keeping her distance from Trump and Vice President…
articles.body:
During a campaign stop in South Carolina last week, President Trump urged Republicans to turn out and vote as if he were on the ballot.

Sen. Susan Collins (R), fighting an uphill re-election battle in blue-leaning Maine, is sending the opposite signal, flexing her independent streak and keeping her distance from Trump and Vice President Vance.

In recent days, she has been the loudest elected Republican criticising Trump’s tariff war with Canada. Earlier this month, Collins was one of two GOP no votes on Todd Blanche, Trump’s new attorney general. And in July, she was a rare voice on the right calling for federal immigration officers to halt non-urgent traffic stops this summer after a deadly shooting in Biddeford, Maine.

Lance Dutson, who served as a senior adviser on Collins’s 2020 Senate reelection and is not involved in her campaign this cycle, said the president served as Collins’s biggest challenge in her reelection.

“The discussion of [Supreme Court Justice Brett] Kavanaugh … or Canadian tariffs or any of these individual issues just absolutely pales in comparison to the general nausea people have about this administration right now,” he said, referring to her deeply controversial vote to confirm the conservative justice despite decades-old sexual assault claims.

Collins was noticeably absent on Monday when Vance rallied the party in Brewer, Maine.

“Senator Collins has a great working relationship with the Vice President,” her campaign told The Hill on Monday in a statement, citing a “personal schedule” that conflicted with Vance’s visit. Dutson also played down the significance of the Vance event.

While Collins has pointed out that she joined Energy Secretary Chris Wright on a recent event promoting an energy storage facility, the dynamic is emblematic of Trump’s drag on Republicans in purple-state races, as his approval ratings hit all-time lows, both overall and on the economy.

Troy Jackson, a logger and former state Senate president who won the Democratic nomination after Graham Platner dropped out, has missed no opportunities to capitalize on the vulnerability.

Commenting on a clip of Vance’s speech on Monday, Jackson noted the vice president “called Susan Collins his ‘dear friend.’ No wonder why — she’s voted for Trump’s agenda 96% of the time.”

Jackson campaign spokesperson Maggie Amjad said in a statement that “Maine voters aren’t stupid, and they see the game that Susan Collins is playing.”

Collins campaign spokesperson Blake Kernen said she puts state over party when it comes to consequential legislation.

“No matter who’s in the White House, Susan Collins works with the president when she agrees with his policies and opposes him when she disagrees,” she said in a statement, noting Collins first spoke out against tariffs on Canada on the Senate floor in April of last year.

Collins is the only Senate Republican running for another term in a state that former Vice President Harris won in 2024.

The Maine Senate race has been caught in some stiff national political winds.

Trump’s approval rating has slid in Maine as it has across the country. According to a University of New Hampshire survey released last month, Trump’s approval rating sits at 40 percent in the state. A separate Reuters/Ipsos poll shows Trump’s national approval rating at 33 percent.

The Trump administration’s tariff policies have also swept up Maine as the U.S. has begun imposing a 50-percent tariff on certain Canadian goods after negotiations fell through late last week. The president took it a step further and threatened to impose tariffs on imported cars, auto parts and aluminum starting in January.

Canada has said it will match U.S. tariffs “dollar for dollar” on a range of American goods – a situation that drew criticism from Collins, whose state borders and does trade with Canada.

“I really want us to go back to the very friendly, economically beneficial relationship that we have with our Canadian neighbors,” Collins told News Center Maine this week. “We produce a lot in Maine — our blueberries, our potatoes, our lobster, our lumber — that is processed across the border. If it comes back with a huge tariff on it, perhaps as much as 50 percent, that increases the cost of eating, building homes and merch[andising] our best-known products.”

On top of that, the party is facing headwinds that presidents in power historically face during the first midterm election of their term.

“You’ve got to give those candidates room to breathe and not try to force yourself onto their shoulders. Stay out of Maine. Give her space to say what she needs to say, do what she needs to do to hold that seat,” said one Republican strategist.

Vance praised Collins for her independent streak on Monday, but jokingly voiced his frustrations over her past breaks with Senate Republicans.

“Whenever I’m in Maine, I’ve got to give Susan a little bit of crap because as you know, Susan is the most independent member of the United States Senate,” the vice president said. “And as the president of the United States Senate, she sometimes makes my job just a little bit harder.”

“But she makes it harder because she is coming to work every single day and fighting not for a political party or not for any abstraction. She comes to work every single day, and she fights for the great people of Maine,” he said.

Vance also gave a shout-out to Maine gubernatorial candidate Bobby Charles, who was also absent. The nonpartisan Cook Political Report rates the state’s governor’s contest as “solid Democratic,” while rating the Senate race as a “toss up.”

The vice president’s remarks are emblematic of the narrow tightrope that Republicans, in particular Collins, have to walk in Maine.

“It’s probably as smart of messaging you can have where he’s almost trying to amplify her independence, but the fact of the matter is, most people in Maine, most voters, aren’t going to pay attention to every word, and slice and dice what the vice president is saying,” the Republican strategist said.

“They’re simply going to see headlines and hear stories that the vice president was in the state campaigning, and probably campaigning for her,” the strategist said. “I don’t think it’s worth the risk to have the vice president or anyone in the admin in that state right now.”

Democrats have sought to portray Collins as a “rubberstamp” for Trump in the Senate, often featuring a picture from Collins, Trump, and other GOP lawmakers in the Oval Office during a bill signing to end the partial government shutdown in February. Trump handed Collins and others a red, MAGA style “America is back!” hat, telling her he heard she was doing “a good job.”

“She voted with Trump 96 percent of the time, was a decisive vote for the Supreme Court nominees that overturned Roe, and even earned the title ‘team player’ amongst her GOP colleagues for being a reliable vote when they need her to push through their destructive policies or nominees. Mainers are sick of it and will vote her out,” said Maddy McDaniel, a spokesperson for the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee.

Dutson said these Democratic attacks were intellectually dishonest, pointing out that they’ve made the same case before — with little success so far.

“We have the quantifiably most independent member of Congress in [Rep.] Jared Golden and the quantifiable most independent member of the United States Senate [in] Susan Collins,” Dutson said, adding “that’s our state’s identity.”

Golden, a Democrat, is not running to re-election. Former Gov. Paul LePage, a loyal Trump ally, is running for the open seat against state Auditor Matthew Dunlap.

Trump has not always been as polite as Vance about Collins’s independent streak.

Earlier this year, Trump laid into Collins over the phone after she supported a Democratic war powers resolution over his actions in Venezuela. And in June, the president referred to Collins, Sens. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska), Rand Paul (R-Ky.), and Bill Cassidy (R-La.) as “losers” after the war senators joined Democrats on a resolution calling on the U.S. to remove troops from Iran.

If Collins survives in November, it won’t be her first time bucking statewide trends against Trump. In 2020, Trump lost Maine by nine points, while Collins won her reelection bid by just over eight points.

The Republican strategist noted that Trump staying away from the race could pay off for him in the long run.

“As maybe embarrassed as you feel by that, and I get it, it’s still a hell of a lot better for Trump and the White House to have her in that Senate seat than the Democrat,” the strategist said.

articles.title: Trump plan to raise borrowing limit on shaky ground as debt roils bond market
articles.summary: President Trump’s plan to raise the debt limit through the end of his presidency before Republicans likely lose control of Congress is on shaky ground because of rising concerns over the national debt — which has reached $40 trillion. The president is quietly pushing Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) and House Speaker Mike Johnson…
articles.body:
President Trump’s plan to raise the debt limit through the end of his presidency before Republicans likely lose control of Congress is on shaky ground because of rising concerns over the national debt — which has reached $40 trillion .

The president is quietly pushing Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) and House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) to use a third budget reconciliation package to extend the debt limit through 2029 — the end of Trump’s term — to avoid the prospect of a difficult negotiation with Democrats next year if they win control of the House or both chambers of Congress.

Yet Trump’s desire to avoid a standoff with Democrats means getting almost all Senate and House Republicans on board with a plan to raise the nation’s borrowing authority by another $5 trillion — and some Republicans say that looks increasingly unlikely.

“If you’re really trying to curb the debt, you wouldn’t do a debt ceiling for two years. You’d try and use it as a lever to change things,” said Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), who warned that Social Security and Medicare will likely need to undergo significant reforms in the next few years to remain solvent.

“You just see interest rates, spending. Every indicator in my mind leads me to believe that before 2032 we’ll have to deal with at least one trust fund if not two that will be insolvent,” he said. “We’ll be incapable of writing a check so you’re going to be forced to do the cuts that we should have been doing the last 12 years.”

Social Security’s trustees warned in a June report that the popular entitlement program is on pace to become insolvent by the end of 2032, which could force as much as a 22 percent cut to benefits.

The program’s trustees moved up the date of insolvency by a year amid annual federal deficits of nearly $2 trillion.

Medicare’s hospital insurance trust fund is projected to become insolvent in 2033, according to the Medicare Trustees annual report from June.

Debt is becoming a bigger political problem as investors demand larger premiums to buy U.S. treasuries, which finance the debt. That in turn is pushing up the costs of mortgages and consumer debt.

The yield on the 30-year Treasury bond reached 5.3 percent last week — the highest level since 2007 — and the average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage hit 6.6 percent.

That spurred Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to announce last week that the Treasury Department would double the limit on how much government debt it is allowed to buy back from investors.

The surprise move temporarily calmed the bond market, but the yield on the 30-year Treasury bond climbed back to 5.2 percent on Thursday and the yield on the 10-year Treasury bond reached 4.7 percent.

Tillis warned that raising the debt limit to cover the final two years of Trump’s presidency would only give both parties more time to ignore the mounting debt, at the risk of leaving Congress on the cusp of a crisis when Trump leaves office in 2029.

“If you do a debt increase of that magnitude, basically give about a 10 or 15 percent debt increase over the current debt level, and you give them two years to spend, it’s going to be a lot worse,” Tillis said.

“We’ll be at [$]45 [trillion] approaching $50 trillion,” he continued, noting that the country’s debt to gross domestic product ratios are “going to be exactly where most economists say the economy stops to function naturally.”

“All those things are additive, I think, to the ultimate economic problem,” the North Carolina senator concluded.

Conservatives in the upper chamber — such as Republican Sens. Rick Scott (Fla.) and Ron Johnson (Wis.), who also chairs the Senate Budget Committee — have argued that inflation is being fueled by excess government spending and persistently high deficits.

Fiscal hawks in Congress warn that Bessent won’t be able to protect long-term U.S. Treasuries and the broader economy from the impact of growing deficits, and they are calling for any debt limit increase to be offset with significant spending cuts.

But any budget reconciliation package with big spending cuts will have a tough time getting the support of 50 GOP senators and 218 House Republicans in the post-election lame-duck session.

This sets up an end-of-year clash between Trump and Republican lawmakers over the debt limit.

Thune says Trump is “keenly interested” in Republicans raising the debt limit again before they potentially lose control of the House after the midterm election.

Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.) is warning that he won’t vote for a budget reconciliation package that raises the debt limit without major spending reforms. He’s pushing his “Six Penny Plan,” which would cut 6 cents off every federal dollar projected to be spent over the next five years.

“We can’t wait any longer. We MUST address our deficit,” Paul recently wrote on social media.

Asked about raising the debt limit, Paul told The Hill: “I’m for less debt, not more.”

“Historically the conservative position has been we don’t vote for the spending that leads to the debt and consequently we also don’t vote for the debt ceiling. People who vote for the spending really need to be the people who vote to raise the debt ceiling,” he said.

Paul marveled that Republicans in Congress used the budget reconciliation process to raise the debt limit by $5 trillion in July 2025 as part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and may be asked to raise it again before the end of the year.

“If we’ve run out of $5 trillion in borrowing power in a year and a half … I don’t know how we got through $5 trillion in a year. That’s crazy,” he said.

Paul reposted on social media a Wall Street Journal op-ed penned by famed investor Stanley Druckenmiller urging the Treasury Department to let bond prices find their natural level.

Druckenmiller, who mentored Bessent early in his career, warned: “You can’t buy your way out of a solvency conversation with liquidity tools. You can only postpone the conversation and raise the eventual price.”

He predicted the Treasury Department would have to expand its bond-buying program substantially to keep yields in check and the expensive endeavor would only postpone the inevitable debt reckoning facing policymakers in Washington.

He argued that the president and lawmakers in Congress should listen to the warning the bond market is sounding over the rising debt.

“Every basis point of artificial yield suppression is a subsidy to procrastination. Suppressed long rates sugarcoat the interest-cost projections, shrink the apparent urgency, and let incumbents assure voters the debt is someone else’s problem,” Druckenmiller wrote.

articles.title: Lindsey Graham's sister wins Republican primary to contest Senate seat in November
articles.summary: The Trump-backed candidate, whose brother Lindsey Graham died in July, has never previously run for elected office.
articles.body:
Voters in South Carolina have chosen Darline Graham, the sister of late Senator Lindsey Graham, as the Republican candidate to contest his US Senate seat in November.

Graham's bid received strong backing from President Donald Trump, who travelled to the state to campaign for her. Graham's victory is being seen as evidence of Trump's continuing influence over the Republican Party.

Graham is currently serving in the Senate as a temporary replacement for her brother, who died suddenly in July. She had never previously run for elected office.

Republicans and Democrats also held primaries in several other states on Tuesday, as they narrowed down their field of candidates for the midterm elections.

Political experts expect that Graham will now go on to succeed in the November election. South Carolina has not elected a Democrat to the Senate for decades.

The midterms more generally will decide which party controls the US Congress - which in turn will have a bearing on the second half of Trump's presidency.

Graham was running against right-wing Republican Congressman Ralph Norman, who sought to portray his opponent as a puppet of Washington politicians.

Lindsey Graham's sister chosen as replacement after senator's death

Curbing Russia, helping Israel and fighting Iran - Lindsey Graham's political identity

The head-to-head was set up after the pair emerged as the top two from a wider field of candidates during an initial contest earlier this month.

Norman is a supporter of Trump and has voted in favour of many of his policies. But in 2024, he initially backed Trump's primary opponent Nikki Haley as his pick for Republican presidential candidate.

With counting almost complete, Graham had received 52.5% of the vote, according to the BBC's US partner CBS News.

In a post on X, she thanked her supporters and the president, and said she was "deeply honoured and humbled" by the result.

During her primary campaign, Graham acknowledged her lack of political experience, particularly after stumbling during a foreign-policy question during a recent debate.

Asked about the US stance towards Taiwan, Graham had said: "I'm not that informed on national security." She added: "National security is not my thing, not my area of expertise, but I do support the military."

Trump's influence over the party was also tested in Oklahoma, where Mike Mazzei, a former state lawmaker endorsed by the president, took on Gentner Drummond, the state's attorney general.

The winner is widely expected to become the next governor in the heavily Republican state.

South Carolina was not the only state that held an election on Tuesday to replace a deceased lawmaker.

In Georgia, voters in the Atlanta area were tasked with choosing a replacement for Democratic Congressman David Scott, who died in April.

Marcye Scott, the daughter of the late congressman, was among those seeking office. But projections in US media show she was beaten by opponent Everton Blair.

Blair will therefore serve out the remainder of the term, which ends in January. In November, two other candidates will run to take over his seat in the new year.

articles.title: Trump is dropping the ball in Venezuela — he needs a new plan
articles.summary: America’s daring Jan. 3 military raid seizing and removing Venezuelan ruler Nicolas Maduro was brilliantly successful. Tragically, however, the Trump administration’s underlying political strategy was flawed from the start. Maduro’s removal changed only the corrupt regime’s public face. The Chavista gang itself remained in power: U.S. acquiescence simply empowered Maduro’s former subordinates, to the detriment…
articles.body:
America’s daring Jan. 3 military raid seizing and removing Venezuelan ruler Nicolas Maduro was brilliantly successful. Tragically, however, the Trump administration’s underlying political strategy was flawed from the start. Maduro’s removal changed only the corrupt regime’s public face.

The Chavista gang itself remained in power: U.S. acquiescence simply empowered Maduro’s former subordinates, to the detriment of Venezuela’s people.

President Trump has had only praise for Maduro’s successor, Delcy Rodriguez. He has called her a “terrific person” and revoked existing U.S. sanctions and blocked Federal investigations against her . He has said that, under her rule, Venezuela is “a happy country .” Venezuelan political polling shows the opposite .

In fact, Trump did a huge favor for Rodriguez and her brother Jorge, head of the puppet National Assembly, by ousting Maduro. Real regime change is now unlikely unless the U.S. and Venezuela’s opposition promptly take decisive steps. That starts when opposition leader Maria Corina Machado is allowed to return home to engage in free, open political activity without intimidation.

The regime’s wholly inadequate response to the severe June earthquakes spurred massive public discontent . Media reports show that government-constructed buildings fared the worst, and that the regime built these structures despite knowing their earthquake vulnerability. Since June, power outages have reached levels not seen since the catastrophic 2019 failure of the national power system . Despite “reforms” to encourage foreign investment in the domestic energy sector, it remains unclear whether thoroughgoing reconstruction is achievable.

So too in the petroleum industry, where resurrection is critical to economic prosperity, and which the White House has touted as ripe for American investment. That has proven false. Major U.S. oil companies, still stung by earlier nationalizations, have hung back. They grasp the considerable capital investments required, and they want a true rule-of-law environment — which is nowhere on the horizon — before making commitments. Instead, there is merely superficial change.

The country’s decayed, decrepit oil infrastructure faces basic chicken-and-egg problems. One example is Venezuela’s port facilities, inadequate for meeting petroleum-export demand, which is especially high now because of the Iran war .

Word-of-mouth reports from interested, small-to-medium-size U.S. drillers is that dealing with Venezuela’s state-owned oil monopoly remains nearly impossible, as it is still unwilling to lessen its iron grip. Even where success is initially reported, deals run into trouble from powerful Venezuelan interests.

Controlling the revenues from oil exports is key. Very little is known either about the offshore U.S. account that receives these revenues initially, or what happens after money is transferred to Venezuela’s central bank. The estimated $13 billion so far seems to have had little effect inside the country . It is unclear whether Washington is not releasing large amounts to Caracas, or the money just disappears once there.

There is no dispute that the Central Bank remains under the Chavista regime’s control. That almost certainly means funds are used to reinforce regime control, aiding supporters and icing out opponents. In short, while superficial U.S. management exists, the regime still makes key decisions on revenue allocation.

Despite (or perhaps because of) these problems, the Rodriguez siblings have entrenched themselves in power while posing as meekly carrying out Washington’s orders. Secretary of State Marco Rubio asserts that he is pressuring the regime toward elections, but proof of real progress is scant.

Observers from the U.S. Council on Foreign Relations and Britain’s Chatham House have called progress toward democratization inadequate . Rubio’s biggest mistake has been sidelining Machado, excluding her from negotiations over possible elections. This is effectively helping Rodriquez divide and conquer the opposition . Even Machado’s gift of her Nobel Peace Prize medallion to Trump has failed to bring him around.

The most obvious evidence the regime is gaming American efforts to move toward elections is that Interior Minister Diosdado Cabello remains firmly in power, and his notorious motorcycle gangs, known as “colectivos,” are still out in force . Any serious democratization plan requires Caballo’s expulsion from office beforehand and the colectivos’ dissolution.

Another imperative is returning all remaining Cuban intelligence and security agents to Havana. Trump correctly stopped Venezuelan oil exports to Cuba, resulting in some agents being shipped home. How many remain, however, is highly unclear , since Cubans have been operating in Venezuela covertly.

Accordingly, Washington must require full transparency from the Rodriguez gang, and high confidence from the U.S. intelligence community when the Cubans are truly gone. Significantly, Washington has an important pressure point for cross-checking whatever Caracas says. Rubio should tell Cuba’s rulers we want full disclosure from them, or their eventual overthrow will only be harder on them, and sooner.

The real centerpiece, however, is Machado’s return home. If, as the White House claims, we control the country, surely we can ensure her safety, and opposition safety generally, including those still awaiting release from prison. We should tell Rodriguez we will hold her personally responsible if any harm comes to Machado. Political liberty and economic recovery in Venezuela will come through pressure, not through the beneficence of the Chavista regime.

John Bolton was national security adviser to President Trump from 2018 to 2019 and U.S. ambassador to the United Nations from 2005 to 2006. He held senior State Department posts at times between1981 and 2005.

articles.title: The left’s constitutional hypocrisy is on full display in its war on Trump
articles.summary: Trump's resistance to judicial rulings on birthright citizenship and tariffs echoes Jefferson, Lincoln and Roosevelt's departmentalist tradition.
articles.body: Progressives have spent months insisting that President Trump is "ignoring the rule of law" whenever he resists or questions judicial rulings — on birthright citizenship, trade policy, the removal of Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook or even the addition of his name to the Kennedy Center. The critique collapses under the weight of the left’s own constitutional commitments. Many of the same people attacking Trump champion popular constitutionalism and departmentalism — two frameworks that explicitly reject judicial supremacy and affirm the independent interpretive authority of the elected branches. In today’s hyper‑politicized legal environment, the left’s selective outrage obscures the constitutional reality. Popular constitutionalism, most famously explicated by former Stanford Law Dean Larry Kramer in "The People Themselves," holds that the people — acting through elected officials — retain ultimate authority over constitutional meaning. Courts are not supreme; they are participants in a broader constitutional conversation. Departmentalism, embraced by presidents from Thomas Jefferson to Richard Nixon, similarly maintains that each branch has an independent duty to interpret the Constitution. GORSUCH SAYS IDEOLOGICAL DIVIDES ON SUPREME COURT COME DOWN TO ‘HOW YOU READ LAW,’ NOT POLITICS Crucially, departmentalism draws a distinction modern critics ignore: while a court’s judgment binds specific parties in a specific case, it does not bind the political branches as a permanent mandate. Rejecting judicial supremacy is not defying the rule of law; it is rejecting the idea that five or six judges have a monopoly on constitutional truth. That view is a mainstream critique of judicial supremacy, yet when Trump invokes the same logic, the left treats departmentalism as dangerous heresy. Trump’s critics speak as though presidential resistance to judicial interpretations is unprecedented, but it is woven into American history. Thomas Jefferson refused to treat Marbury v. Madison as binding beyond the parties, writing that "each of the three departments has equally the right to decide for itself what is its duty under the Constitution." Andrew Jackson declared the Supreme Court’s views "ought not to control the coordinate authorities of this government." Abraham Lincoln treated Dred Scott v. Sandford as binding only on the immediate litigants, refusing to accept it as a permanent rule for the nation. Franklin Roosevelt openly challenged the Court’s constitutional interpretations during the New Deal, and Richard Nixon frequently asserted independent executive authority in administrative matters. If presidential resistance to judicial supremacy were inherently lawless, half of America’s most consequential presidents would be guilty of it. LIBERAL STATE SUPREME COURT JUSTICE BLASTS SCOTUS CONSERVATIVES, SAYS HAWAII WILL DEFY HIGH COURT Trump’s actions fall squarely within this tradition. Much of today’s friction stems not from executive defiance of individual decrees, but from lower courts relying on nationwide injunctions that attempt to freeze executive action everywhere at once. That modern dynamic makes departmentalist principles more relevant than ever. The Supreme Court’s recent jurisprudence has pushed back against such injunctions, emphasizing that lower courts exceed their constitutional authority when they attempt to issue sweeping rules binding the entire government. That judicial self‑restraint aligns directly with departmentalism: the judiciary’s role is to resolve specific disputes between specific litigants, not to govern coequal branches. Critics point to Trump’s continuing efforts to end birthright citizenship as proof of lawlessness. But the dispute is fundamentally about constitutional interpretation. Although the Supreme Court recently ruled against Trump’s position, pressing the argument again through distinct legal channels reflects the same iterative process past presidents used when they believed the Court misread the Constitution. TRUMP CRITICIZES 2 SUPREME COURT JUSTICES BY NAME OVER TARIFF RULING The same dynamic defines recent tariff disputes. When the Supreme Court ruled in Learning Resources v. Trump that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act did not delegate unilateral tariff-setting authority, the administration’s pivot to alternative statutory mechanisms was labeled lawlessness. But testing other delegations passed by Congress is standard interbranch dialogue. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION The rule of law does not require presidents to treat judicial interpretations as infallible. It requires them to operate within constitutional limits — and assert their own constitutional judgments when appropriate. President Trump is doing exactly that. This isn’t an abstract point for me. Long before Donald Trump entered national politics, I wrote a book published by Oxford University Press making the historical case against popular constitutionalism and departmentalism — an originalist defense of judicial finality. But that scholarly position does not mean President Trump is ignoring the rule of law or behaving like an authoritarian when he advances a theory of judicial review that other presidents and scholars have likewise advanced. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The real danger is not presidential resistance to judicial supremacy — it is the selective outrage that turns constitutional theory into a partisan weapon.

articles.title: ‘Captain Canada’ firebrand unloads on Trump with profane one-liner as trade war escalates
articles.summary: Ontario Premier Doug Ford told President Donald Trump to "kiss my a--" on CP24 after Trump mocked him as less impressive than late brother Rob Ford.
articles.body: A simmering trade rift between President Donald Trump and Canadian officials burst into the open Monday as Ontario Premier Doug Ford sharply escalated his attacks on the president amid a widening tariff fight between the longtime allies. "He can kiss my a-- as far as I’m concerned. We’re going to go at him full steam, and we buy 400% more cars than anyone in the world," Ford said in an interview with Toronto radio station Newstalk 1010 Monday in response to Trump’s threat of new tariffs on Canadian autos, auto parts and steel. Trump mocked Ford on Monday as "less charismatic, intelligent, and overall unimpressive" than his late brother, former Toronto Mayor Rob Ford, who became embroiled in a major 2013 scandal over his use of crack cocaine, which he later admitted. The Ontario premier, dubbed "Captain Canada," has since emerged as one of the country’s most outspoken critics of Trump’s trade threats. TRUMP TRADE CHIEF WARNS CANADA WALKED AWAY FROM 'THE BEST DEAL' TO TRIGGER 50% U.S. TARIFFS The tariff fight is unfolding on two tracks: new 50% U.S. tariffs on certain Canadian goods took effect Aug. 22, with Canada set to retaliate Sept. 8, while Trump separately threatened to raise tariffs on Canadian autos and auto parts to 50% beginning Jan. 1, 2027. The White House referred Fox News Digital to Trump’s Truth Social posts when approached for additional comment. "America has been carrying Canada for decades, but no longer! The U.S.A. will always be far bigger, richer, and stronger than Canada. Without the United States, Canada couldn’t survive — It’s where they get all of their money and, because of their current bad leadership, primarily Governor Carney, and his Flunky, Ford, they will not be allowed to keep taking advantage of the United States — Their key to survival," Trump added in a post. TRUMP MUST CLOSE THE BACK DOOR CHINA USES TO EXPLOIT NORTH AMERICAN TRADE He claimed Canada imposes tariffs of 400% or more on U.S. farmers and said he plans to end what he describes as unfair trade treatment of American companies and producers. Trump also threatened further economic pressure, claiming much of the electricity, oil and gas Canada receives is transported through the U.S. and calling on the country to "fall in line." CANADA REPORTEDLY SCRAPS JOINT BRIDGE CELEBRATION WITH US AFTER TRUMP RENEWS TARIFF THREAT Beyond tariffs, Trump also escalated the rhetoric Tuesday by floating a proposal to rename Lake Ontario "Lake America." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The current tariff fight traces back to late 2024, when Trump threatened 25% tariffs on Canadian goods and later joked during a meeting with then-Prime Minister Justin Trudeau that Canada could become the 51st state. Fox News Digital reached out to Ford for comment.

articles.title: California Dems trigger outrage after siding with convicted child sex offenders in shocking vote
articles.summary: California Senate Democrats rejected a Republican effort to ban all sex offender registry tiers from holding public office, including school board seats, in a party-line vote.
articles.body: California Senate Democrats rejected Republican Sen. Suzette Valladares’ effort to close a "loophole" allowing some people convicted of sex crimes against minors to seek public office, including school board seats. At issue is AB 2691, a proposal to add sexual assault and human trafficking to the felony convictions that disqualify Californians from elected office. Valladares’ amendment sought to undo Democratic-led changes that allow people convicted of certain sex crimes against minors to remain eligible to seek public office. "Right now in California, someone convicted of sexually abusing a child can still sit on your school board. That's not a loophole. That's a choice. And in my perspective, and most, that's wrong," Valladares, R-Santa Clarita, said on the California Senate floor while urging colleagues to adopt an amendment that Senate Democrats later rejected on a party-line vote, according to her office. "Predators who sexually abuse children have no place holding public office. None, not in the Capitol, not on city council, and definitely not on our school boards. AB 2691 was supposed to guarantee that. It started as a simple ban," she continued. "Convicted sex offenders don't get to hold public office. Period. But amendments added this summer gutted it, narrowing the bill to cover only tier three offenders and deliberately exempting tier one and tier two." SEX CRIMES COULD COST LAWMAKERS TAXPAYER-FUNDED PENSIONS UNDER HAWLEY’S NEW PROPOSAL Under the bill’s current language, the new public-office ban would apply to sexual-assault convictions requiring lifetime Tier 3 sex-offender registration. People whose convictions place them in Tier 1 or Tier 2 — categories requiring at least 10 or 20 years on the registry before they can ask a court for removal — would not be disqualified under the proposed law. Concern was also raised months ago during a Senate committee hearing, when Republican California state Sen. Steven Choi asked Assemblywoman Dawn Addis, the bill’s Democratic author, why people convicted of certain sex crimes against minors could remain eligible to seek office under the amended measure. Addis did not address the specific offenses Choi identified, instead calling AB 2691 a "first in the nation" proposal that would protect survivors and saying she was open to working with lawmakers on other crimes. "We're doing a first in the nation bill that would protect the public trust of survivors and would make sure that survivors are really in the lead," Addis responded. "Happy to continue working with the committee or others if there are other kinds of crimes folks feel need to be addressed. But at the moment, I feel like we have a really important bill that is nation leading, that will uplift survivors and enhance public trust here in California." DRAG QUEEN SCHOOL BOARD VICE PRESIDENT ARRESTED ON CHILD PORNOGRAPHY AND ENDANGERMENT CHARGES California state Sen. Scott Wiener, the Democratic chair of the committee that considered the bill, argued that a broader prohibition based on all three registry tiers would be overbroad. He said California’s registry had historically included both "sexually violent predator[s]" and others who have committed less serious crimes, citing an example of "a gay guy who had sex in a park or in a car and got arrested." "Sex offender registry is not punishment," Wiener argued. "It is a tool for law enforcement to be able to monitor people who may potentially cause a risk. And when we use the sex offender registry as a proxy for anything else, we get into problems." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP But Sen. Valladares told Fox News Digital that the issue "isn't complicated" for her. "I’m a mom. This one isn’t complicated for me. Today, 40 senators had the chance to say convicted sex offenders should NEVER hold public office in California," she told Fox News Digital. "Ten Republicans stood up to vote for what is right. My amendments would have closed the door. No loopholes. No exceptions. No convicted sex offenders serving in positions of public trust, including on our school boards. Protecting our kids should NEVER be partisan. I’m deeply disappointed, and I’m not done fighting."

Darline Graham’s (R-S.C.) narrow victory in South Carolina’s Senate primary runoff makes her the heavy favorite to win the seat for a full term in November, but some Democrats see a narrow…
articles.body:
Sen. Darline Graham ’s (R-S.C.) narrow victory in South Carolina’s Senate primary runoff makes her the heavy favorite to win the seat for a full term in November, but some Democrats see a narrow opening for an upset.

Graham fended off a challenge from Rep. Ralph Norman (R-S.C.) in the Tuesday contest, having been boosted by President Trump ’s endorsement. She’s on track to win the race by about 5 points, overcoming late scrutiny for a gaffe she made during a debate with Norman in which she said she isn’t “that informed on national security.”

Graham is now set to face pediatrician Annie Andrews in the general election. The incumbent will be favored given South Carolina’s solid red lean — Democrats haven’t won a Senate seat in the Palmetto State since 1998.

But facing off against a candidate whose inexperience has become a key issue in the minds of many voters has given some Democrats a shot of optimism.

“Darline Graham is hilariously unprepared to be a senator, which gives Democrats a tremendous opening to flip the seat. It’ll be a tough fight, but Annie Andrews is great and has a real shot,” said Democratic strategist Mike Nellis in a post on the social platform X .

Andrews easily prevailed in the Democratic primary in June but has been waiting for weeks to find out her opponent since the sudden death of former Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.).

During a podcast episode that aired Tuesday, Andrews said she expects “record-breaking” Democratic turnout.

“When you have a motivated Democratic base in a state like South Carolina in a midterm year, that spells trouble for the GOP because we have a motivated base,” she told the hosts of “Nobody Knows Anything.”

“I’m a disciplined candidate. I’m going to be talking about affordability every single day because that’s what voters care about, and those are the real problems I’m hearing from the people I’m talking to on the ground,” she added. “But I do think the anti-Darlene argument becomes the anti-nepotism argument that she’s not ready for this.”

Andrews, who lost a 2022 House race to Rep. Nancy Mace (R), has a bit of a head start to introduce herself to voters, though Graham inherits massive name recognition from her brother.

“National Democrats – South Carolina is now a real pick-up opportunity with @AnnieAndrewsMD running against this incurious ignoramus,” said Patrice Snow , who formerly served as press secretary for Tom Steyer ’s 2020 presidential campaign and a PAC founded by former Massachusetts Gov. Deval Patrick (D).

Snow called on Democrats to provide Andrews with the “resources she needs to flip this seat.”

Andrews has so far put up decent fundraising numbers. Her most recent campaign filing at the end of the second quarter of 2026 showed she had raised nearly $11 million so far, with $4 million in cash on hand.

Andrews’s campaign sent a fundraising text out to South Carolinians on Tuesday night attacking Graham, The Post and Courier reporter Ian Grenier reported .

“This is a woman running for an office only 100 Americans get the responsibility of holding,” the message reads. “The Senate isn’t the place for on the job training.”

The sentiment echoes the message that Norman sought to make against Graham.

Norman conceded his loss to Graham on Tuesday and said he would do what he can to support her candidacy. But he said “Democrats got what they wanted” in facing her in the general election.

Still, Graham will be far from lacking resources. Money poured in to boost her in the primary, including more than $800,000 from Trump’s super PAC, MAGA Inc.

South Carolina also isn’t essential to Democrats’ plans to win back a majority in the Senate, and some may feel their money would be better spent elsewhere in states that aren’t seen as much of a traditional uphill battle.

Democrats were bullish about their chances of pulling off an upset against Lindsey Graham in 2020 behind Jaime Harrison , only for Harrison to lose by 10 points.

But if some of the skepticism about Darline Graham’s qualifications fester and Andrews is able to tap into that, the race could be closer, especially in what’s expected to be a strong Democratic year.

The “9 to 5” star, who famously avoided politics, “died peacefully” at 80 years old in Nashville, Tenn., her publicity team announced , remembering her “a rhinestone life that shone bright enough for the world to see.”

“Dolly will forever stand as an inspiration not only through her timeless music and prolific songwriting, but also her wit, warmth, and kindness that made us all feel like family,” the announcement read.

“This is a true loss for millions of people. There has never been anyone like her, and never will,” the president wrote on his Truth Social platform .

Several governors followed suit, ordering flags flown at half mass throughout their states to honor Parton, including Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear (D), Mississippi Gov. Tate Reeves (R), Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine (R) and Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R).

Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee (R) celebrated the proud Tennessean as a “rare” example of someone “who climbs to the pinnacle of fame, then scoffs at its allure only to retain the genuine humility that defines them.

Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) said Parton was “one of the great entertainers of our era,” while New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) called her “an extraordinary person and an irreplaceable champion of the working class.”

EYE-OPENING REPORT : A major study of former NFL players who died during a five-year period found at least a quarter of them had chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), the brain disease that has been found in dozens of other former players.

The report from the British Medical Journal released Tuesday examined brains of former NFL players who died between 2008 and 2021, zeroing in on the six-year span between 2016 and 2021, when donations were the highest. Analyzing 235 brains from that span, researchers diagnosed 215 of them with CTE.

That would be 24.5 percent of the total 878 former NFL players who died between those years. But researchers said the prevalence could be much higher for that span, as they were unable to analyze the other 643 players whose brains were not donated.

The possible prevalence of CTE could be as high as about 97 percent, but the true number is likely somewhere between 25 and 97 percent, the research team said.

The report adds the latest round of scrutiny on the impacts of repeated hits to the head and injuries on the long-term health of NFL players.

The NFL has faced backlash in recent decades after the suicides and other deaths of several high-profile players who were later confirmed to be suffering from CTE. The disease, which the Mayo Clinic attributes to repeated head trauma, can only be diagnosed after someone’s death, though some symptoms are known.

The disease can cause emotional distress, mood swings, memory loss and difficulty thinking. The study also found those with the most advanced stage of CTE also had dementia.

The controversy surrounding the NFL’s safety protocols around head injuries was recounted in the 2015 film “Concussion.”

The NFL told ESPN in response to the study that it “continuously strives to make the game of football safer, including by implementing strategies to reduce concussions and head impacts.”

The NFL Players Association said the study is a “a sobering reminder that football carries real risks, and those risks can have lasting consequences for players and their families.”

MEASLES DEATHS : Two unvaccinated people from Pennsylvania died from measles , the state’s health department said Tuesday, marking the first two U.S. deaths from the contagious virus this year.

The deaths also mark the first measles-related deaths in Pennsylvania in 35 years.

“Because measles was largely eliminated in the Commonwealth for more than three decades, people are not familiar with this disease and don’t fully understand the potential severity of the illness,” Pennsylvania Secretary of Health Debra Bogen said in a statement.

She encouraged residents to get the MMR vaccine, which, she said, “is safe and provides the best protection we have against measles.”

The department said both individuals were residents of Lancaster County but declined to provide additional identifying information about them.

The U.S. has recently seen a resurgence in measles cases, and the latest deaths bring the total to five deaths in the last two years, which is more than the combined total of measles-related deaths from the three decades before that.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported 2,777 cases in 2026 alone, as of last Thursday, which is already more than the total from 2025. The developments coincide with the Trump administration’s effort to scale back childhood vaccine requirements.

Trump is pushing to break up the MMR vaccine into multiple shots, requiring more visits to the doctor, which health experts say will reduce uptake. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has sent mixed messages about the safety of the vaccine.

Authorities allege Culver claimed in January to be a “Special Master enforcing orders” of the Supreme Court to pressure a judge in Lake County, Ind., to drop criminal cases against him.
