articles.title: What the Supreme Court’s mail ballot ruling means
articles.summary: The Supreme Court’s mail-in voting ruling on Monday in favor of President Trump stirred up the dust just ahead of the midterms. “Only time will tell,” the court cautioned on the lawfulness of Trump’s policy in question as it ruled on an early challenge to it. Mail ballots are set to go out in a matter of days. And the battle could quickly boomerang to the high court. To hear some prominent Democrats tell…
articles.body:
The Supreme Court’s mail-in voting ruling on Monday in favor of President Trump stirred up the dust just ahead of the midterms.

“Only time will tell,” the court cautioned on the lawfulness of Trump’s policy in question as it ruled on an early challenge to it.

Mail ballots are set to go out in a matter of days. And the battle could quickly boomerang to the high court.

To hear some prominent Democrats tell it, the justices have already upended the midterms. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) called it a “dagger into the heart of our democracy.” Former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.) described it as an “insult to the vision of our founders.”

Others in the party were more measured. Sen. Dick Durbin (D-Ill.), the ranking member of the Senate Judiciary Committee, described the ruling as just a “temporary procedural win” for Trump. Norm Eisen , whose group has filed dozens of lawsuits against Trump, told his followers on social media, “Please don’t overreact.”

Let’s start with what the Supreme Court actually ruled in its apparent 6-3 vote:

First, the justices said blue states have no legal standing, meaning their right to sue, over Trump’s executive order. The court found the order itself doesn’t cause the states any concrete harm.

Second, the justices ruled the case unripe. They] said any hypothetical injuries wouldn’t happen until the U.S. Postal Service (USPS) implements the president’s directive. The agency’s final plan is being formally published Wednesday.

They did not decide whether who may eventually have standing once USPS moves forward, or if it will be legal.

That’s why some blue states still sound confident, despite their loss.

New York Attorney General Letitia James (D) called the Supreme Court’s decision a “setback.” Washington Attorney General Nick Brown (D) said it merely meant his office must wait “slightly longer.” And others, including Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D), took issue with headlines suggesting the court had greenlit Trump’s policy.

“Not so fast. Today’s SCOTUS decision does NOT deal with the substance of Trump’s unconstitutional Executive Order and does not mean his illegal attempt to restrict mail-in voting will go forward,” Shapiro wrote on social media.

There’s no clear answer yet as to how much of Trump’s policy can be implemented for November’s elections. Expect the next word to come from U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani , an appointee of former President Obama who serves on the federal trial bench in Boston.

While one block was lifted, Trump’s executive order remains blocked nationwide under a second injunction Talwani issued. That case is a separate lawsuit from the states’ case. It’s filed by the League of Women Voters of Massachusetts and wasn’t directly before the Supreme Court, so the block technically remains in effect. The organization says it should stay put.

“We will fight to keep it that way or to secure new relief,” the league said in a statement.

But the Justice Department (DOJ) wants it gone, saying in court filings that “the Supreme Court’s order leaves no room for any further dispute.” The judge had no authority, so she’s compelled to wipe her ruling, DOJ argues.

Side with Trump: The judge agrees to lift her remaining injunction and refuses requests from both the blue states and the voting group to intervene again. It would pave the way for the Trump administration to implement as much of its policy as it can before mail ballots go out.

Enforce the existing injunction: The judge rules her existing injunction in the voting group’s case withstands the Supreme Court’s decision. She agrees the executive order and any steps to implement it must remain blocked.

Issue a new injunction: The judge agrees her existing injunction must be tossed. However, now that USPS has finalized its new policy, she issues a new block preventing further implementation.

Do nothing: The judge continues to consider the parties’ arguments, leaving her existing injunction in effect.

DOJ demanded Talwani agree to the first option by Tuesday evening, a deadline she declined.

The clock is ticking. Mail ballots in some states begin going out in less than two weeks. And USPS’ final rule implementing Trump’s executive order is slated to be published in the Federal Register on Wednesday, so it can go into effect immediately if the courts get out of the way.

The administration is threatening to immediately start climbing the appellate ladder to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 1 st Circuit if Talwani doesn’t side with them.

Meanwhile, Democratic Party leaders are making moves of their own. They, too, had filed a legal challenge. But it was brought in the nation’s capital, where judges rejected it. On Tuesday evening, they filed a new motion asking to stop the USPS from carrying out its newly finalized plan.

The 95-page document makes some previous ballot recommendations required. Mail ballots must include an official logo, unique barcodes with the person’s ZIP code embedded and other specifications. Designs must be submitted to a federal design analyst.

Local or state election officials also must upload voters’ names and addresses into a portal, though it doesn’t collect birthdates or Social Security numbers.

USPS will intervene if a state sends a ballot to someone without uploading their information to the portal. However, the rule stresses the agency isn’t consulting external databases at the Department of Homeland Security or elsewhere. The data comes from state and local election officials.

“The Postal Service will not second-guess the states’ submissions,” the rule reads. “State election officials will thus retain full control over who is permitted to vote in federal elections in their state by U.S. mail.”

The fight over whether Trump’s name can be legally added to the facade of the renowned Kennedy Center is far from over.

On Thursday, it will be back in the hands of U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper .

Cooper ruled in May that the institution’s board — handpicked and chaired by Trump — unlawfully voted to rename the building and ordered the lettering of the president’s name be removed. He also temporarily blocked plans for a two-year closure for renovations.

The administration ultimately complied after unsuccessful attempts to fight the order, and Trump’s name was stripped overnight in mid-June only to be obscured from view by a tarp.

Democrats hailed the removal as a symbolic win for “democracy and the rule of law,” seemingly closing this chapter of the president’s efforts to remake the nation’s capital in his image.

That is until earlier this month when the board again approved adding a reference to Trump underneath the Kennedy Center name, this time in the form of an inscription that reads: “Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump.” It also revived closure plans and voted to rename a plaza after Trump.

Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio), an ex-officio board member who has long been fighting the changes in court, quickly challenged the new resolution. Her lawyers argued it “openly flouts” the court’s previous order and asked Cooper in an emergency motion to “put an end to this childish gambit.”

The Kennedy Center has said that it would hold off on the changes until at least Sept. 8 while the legal process continues to play out.

Late Monday, the Justice Department (DOJ) asserted the board’s decision was entirely lawful and did not run afoul of Cooper’s order because the center would continue to bear the congressionally mandated “John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts” name.

The DOJ filing paints the picture of an institution in “terminal decline,” one that is bleeding cash and in desperate need of repairs. It lauds Trump as the “sole hope” for the center’s long-term survival, pointing to his efforts to procure donors for an endowment fund.

“An order blocking the Board from appropriately recognizing President Trump will cause donors to flee, financial contributions to dry up, and structural rehabilitation to stop,” DOJ attorneys wrote. “There will simply not be the expertise or funding necessary to rebuild and renovate this decimated structure.”

“The Trump Administration is ready to go but, without it, the Kennedy Center cannot be saved,” they added.

Nathaniel Zelensky , who is representing Beatty, criticized the DOJ’s suggestion that the building could be at risk as a “not-to-so-subtle threat to demolish the Kennedy Center if [the] President doesn’t get his way.”

“This is unconscionable; it is unbecoming of the Department of Justice to even put this in a filing, and we will answer in court,” Zelinsky, the principal and managing counsel of the Washington Litigation Group, told The Gavel in a statement.

Both parties will be in Cooper’s courtroom for a 2 p.m. EDT hearing on Thursday, as he weighs whether the board can move forward with its plans.

Don’t be surprised if additional hearings are scheduled throughout the week. But here’s what we’re watching for now:

articles.title: Pentagon attack on Stars and Stripes is part of Trump’s war on media
articles.summary: The Trump administration has implemented measures to restrict independent journalism, including the firing of leadership at the military newspaper Stars and Stripes following reports on poor conditions aboard the aircraft carrier Abraham Lincoln.
articles.body:
The Aug. 21 firing of the publisher, editor and a reporter at the military newspaper Stars and Stripes, along with recent restrictions on what the paper can publish, are examples of the Trump administration’s efforts to limit what Americans can learn about government actions.

The firings came soon after Stars and Stripes reported on harsh conditions — including food and water shortages, and malfunctioning plumbing — experienced by sailors deployed since November on the aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln, which was participating in President Trump’s war of choice against Iran. The newspaper reported that some sailors were “struggling with exhaustion and declining morale, including reports of suicidal thoughts.”

Trump denied the reports and falsely claimed the carrier was “beautifully maintained and beautifully taken care of.” He accurately said it was soon heading back to the U.S.

Following the playbook of foreign dictatorships where freedom of the press doesn’t exist, Trump and his appointees are doing all they can to cover up their many failures and spread propaganda touting their false claims of success.

The Freedom of the Press Foundation has documented a long list of actions Trump and his administration have taken to “defund, defang and silence independent reporting.”

These actions include multibillion-dollar lawsuits Trump has filed against news organizations that reported unflattering stories about him. Other actions include the ending of federal funding of NPR and PBS, the near-dissolution of government broadcaster Voice of America, the ban on journalists Trump dislikes from the White House press pool and threats by the Trump-appointed chair of the Federal Communications Commission to revoke broadcast licenses of television stations owned by networks that air criticism of Trump.

Trump wants us to believe that whatever preposterous lies he tells — such as his claim that he won the 2020 presidential election — are true, while whatever truthful reporting he denounces is false. His low approval ratings in polls show many Americans have stopped believing him.

The firings at Stars and Stripes and restrictions the Defense Department has imposed on the newspaper deprive American service members who have volunteered to risk their lives defending our nation of their right to get accurate and independent news about the military, our government, the nation and the world.

Stars and Stripes staffers are civilian employees of the Defense Department, which partially funds the publication. A 1993 department directive says the paper shall provide “a free flow of news and information to its readership without news management or censorship. The calculated withholding of unfavorable news is prohibited.”

The Pentagon ended that policy in January. Defense Department spokesman Sean Parnell wrote on social media that the department “will modernize” Stars and Stripes to “refocus its content away from woke distractions that syphon morale, and adapt it to serve a new generation of service members.”

In addition, Parnell wrote that Stars and Stripes must no longer publish stories produced by The Associated Press , a nonpartisan news service with reporters around the world that provides news to thousands of newspapers, broadcasters and websites. This severely limits the news Stars and Stripes can publish.

These changes aren’t about modernization. They are about censorship, giving the Defense Department the power to run Stars and Stripes as a propaganda organ that reports only news favorable to the Trump administration.

When the newspaper’s ombudsman warned that the new policy endangered its editorial independence, she was fired , prompting her to file a lawsuit against the Defense Department in June.

The editorial independence of Stars and Stripes dates back to World War I. Gen. John Pershing said the paper helped “sustain the morale” of troops because it was uncensored and truthful. During World War II, Gen. Dwight Eisenhower said that “Stars and Stripes is the soldiers’ newspaper. We will not interfere.”

Stars and Stripes has been continuously published since World War II as a daily tabloid and has appeared online since 2004. Before the internet and smartphones, it was often the only source of news for many members of the military stationed abroad.

Trump seeks to portray most of the news media as dishonest, far-left and anti-American. He has called the news media “an enemy of the American people,” echoing the charge dictators Adolf Hitler of Germany, Josef Stalin of the Soviet Union, and Mao Zedong of China made against independent news organizations in their countries.

In fact, the media function as the eyes and ears of the American people, shedding light on government actions to hold officials accountable, regardless of political party.

Every president has clashed with the media. The relationship between the two is inherently adversarial. But Trump has done more than any modern president — even Richard Nixon — to seek to muzzle journalists and news organizations in order to limit unfavorable news coverage.

Our 80-year-old president won’t change his hostility to independent media. We should all hope that whoever becomes president in 2029 embraces the dramatically different view expressed in 1786 by future president Thomas Jefferson, who wrote : “Our liberty depends on the freedom of the press, and that cannot be limited without being lost.”

A. Scott Bolden is an attorney, NewsNation contributor, former chair of the Washington, D.C. Democratic Party and a former New York state prosecutor.

articles.body:
Three U.S. Secret Service (USSS) officials were placed on administrative leave Tuesday amid an investigation into possible misconduct, a spokesperson told The Hill.

The agency’s Office of Professional Responsibility is conducting the probe, and details around the investigation were not immediately clear. All three officials were non-law enforcement personnel, according to the spokesperson.

“The U.S. Secret Service is committed to upholding the highest standards of professionalism and integrity in fulfilling our zero-fail mission of protecting the President and other high-level government officials,” they said in a statement.

“Our critical work demands that our workforce maintain an unwavering commitment to duty, honesty, and courage in all aspects of their jobs,” the statement continued. “We will continue to pursue the level of excellence that is worthy of the mission which has been entrusted to us by the American people.”

Last month, a Secret Service agent assigned to Vice President Vance was put on administrative leave for allegedly leaking sensitive information. This followed reporting from MS Now about frustrations from Vance’s security detail over last-minute trips and assignments, which cited unnamed current and former USSS agents and administration officials.

The agency has also faced public scrutiny amid multiple assassination plots against President Trump, including the attempted attack at the White House Correspondents’ Association Dinner in April.

The Secret Service was also involved in the secret transfer of the president from the old Air Force One to another plane while departing Turkey last month amid an Iranian threat. Some of his staff and the press corps remained on the other plane and were unaware of the situation.

The event sparked concerns about Trump’s safety while traveling abroad.

articles.title: Migrant shops shut doors in pre-election protest against Germany's AfD
articles.summary: Businesses run by migrants in the German city of Magdeburg closed their doors for several hours on Wednesday in protest against the anti-migrant Alternative...
articles.body:
Businesses run by migrants in the German city of Magdeburg closed their doors for several hours on Wednesday in protest against the anti-migrant Alternative for Germany (AfD), which is leading the polls ahead of an election in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt.

A rally outside the state parliament was also planned for Wednesday.

"What is important to us is this: Nobody should have to prove through work or economic output that they belong to this society," said Saeeid Saeeid of the Saxony-Anhalt refugee council.

Around 150 businesses in the area around one of Magdeburg's central squares, Hasselbachplatz, including restaurants, barbershops and kiosks, took part in the strike, closing from 10 am to 3 pm (0800-1300 GMT), an organizer said. Businesses not owned by migrants also planned to join the strike.

Saeeid said there was "an extraordinary sense of solidarity" within the community. "Business owners are motivating one another, joining forces and peacefully raising their voices against racism and exclusion."

The aim is to draw attention to what would be missing if migrant-run businesses did not exist, a co-organizer said. Migrants keep care services running, deliver parcels, and work in construction and industry, she said.

"But we don't want to be seen only as workers, but as people with all their needs," said the organizer, who works as a social worker.

She said the strike was meant to be a wake-up call to society and an appeal to look closely at the AfD's programme.

Saxony-Anhalt elects a new state parliament on September 6. The state's AfD branch, which is classified as a far-right extremist group by the domestic intelligence agency, currently leads the polls and is seeking an absolute majority to lead a state parliament for the first time.

Against the backdrop of the state elections in Saxony-Anhalt and the AfD's poll numbers, migrant business owners in Magdeburg are going on strike on August 26. articles.title: Reform proposes £30 tax rebate for HMRC phone delays
articles.summary: People on hold to HMRC for more than 30 minutes would get a tax credit under plans announced by Robert Jenrick.
articles.body:
People on hold to HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) for more than 30 minutes would get £30 off their tax bill under a Reform UK government, Robert Jenrick has announced.

Reform's economy spokesman said HMRC's treatment of taxpayers was "offensive to working people" and his party would tie the pay of senior HMRC officials to customer service targets.

To prevent abuse, the tax credit for phone delays would be limited to two occasions in a given tax year, Jenrick said.

HMRC has said it has improved its response times since a highly critical report by a committee of MPs , external , in January 2025, accused the organisation of seeking to "degrade its telephone service to drive taxpayers to digital channels".

The Public Accounts Committee report said nearly 44,000 customers were cut off without warning after being on hold for more than an hour in 2024 and "HMRC's treatment of taxpayers has damaged trust in the tax system".

Jenrick highlighted the findings - which were rejected as "completely baseless" by the then boss of HMRC - at a media conference in central London.

"Frankly, it is offensive to working people and I have had enough," said the former Tory MP.

"So, we will give HMRC a big incentive to actually provide proper customer service.

"I'm announcing today that under a Reform government, if you spend more than half an hour waiting for HMRC to answer your call, you will get a £30 credit off your tax bill. If HMRC delay, they can repay.

"And to make sure that the staff actually hit their targets, we'll tie the pay of senior HMRC officials to their customer service performance."

Jenrick also pledged to scrap UK privacy rules in favour of a "light-touch" approach to data protection as part of a bid to slash "red tape" for businesses.

He said the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), which mirrors EU legislation and was adopted as domestic law after Brexit, had "strangled" tech firms and small enterprises.

The framework would be replaced by rules modelled on New Zealand's privacy legislation, which Reform says has the lightest-touch regime still recognised as being "adequate" by the EU.

Labour accused Reform of wanting to "scrap vital safeguards that protect people's private data" with its "unworkable and unserious plans".

He has that right; that’s his prerogative,” Norman said, eliciting loud boos from the crowd. The…
articles.body:
Supporters of Rep. Ralph Norman (R-S.C.) did not hold back their frustration with President Trump during the Senate candidate’s concession speech on Tuesday evening after he was defeated Tuesday in South Carolina’s GOP primary runoff.

“The president got involved. He has that right; that’s his prerogative,” Norman said, eliciting loud boos from the crowd.

The lawmaker responded by telling those gathered that Trump’s “policies are good,” but the Republican said he “never understood” why the president got involved in the race.

“But it is what it is, and I’ll accept it,” he continued. “I’ve always said, something good will come out of this. I don’t know what it is, but something good will come out of it.”

Darline Graham, the sister of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), secured a victory in the state primary. She was tapped to fill out the remainder of her brother’s term after his sudden death last month.

Trump later encouraged her to seek a full, six-year term in the Senate after the pair met in the Oval Office shortly after the late senator’s death, calling her a “spectacular person” and “a true American Patriot.” She launched her campaign soon after.

Norman, who was flanked by his family on stage, committed during his Tuesday speech to supporting Graham in the general election.

The Republican nominee will face Democrat Annie Andrews, a Charleston pediatrician, in November. The Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan election forecaster, rates this race as “solidly Republican.”

While Norman expressed gratitude to the South Carolinians who supported his campaign, he did not hold back his disappointment at the election result.

“I hate it for the state. I really hate it for the state,” he said. “I don’t hate it for me. I don’t hate it for the family.”

“We’re going to be fine, but we did this for service, and I hate it for the state,” the lawmaker added. “But the public, South Carolina, made their decision.”

articles.title: Republicans have sacrificed Milton Friedman’s free market on the altar of Trump
articles.summary: Today’s Republicans seem to have forgotten Friedman’s lesson in the market-distorting and economy-threatening effects of business-government collusion.
articles.body:
In late July, the Trump administration announced it would take equity stakes worth nearly $1 billion in seven more private semiconductor companies as part of its investment in domestic chipmaking capacity. For those keeping track, President Trump’s government has now taken ownership stakes in 30 companies since first demanding a 10 percent share of Intel last year.

For a guy who loves to attack Democrats as communists, Trump’s spree of government ownership in private industry has little parallel in modern American history. As the line separating the free market from government blurs, a growing number of executives — most of them in the increasingly overlapping Big Tech and surveillance sectors — are happily surrendering their inch-deep belief in the free market for a double scoop of political influence.

Trump’s interest in taking ownership stakes in AI companies is well-known, and it speaks volumes about how quickly the Republican Party has abandoned the free market principles of its one-time prophet, economist Milton Friedman . If Democrats want to craft a sound and effective criticism of Trump’s China-style government buying spree, they should look to Friedman’s many warnings about what happens when Big Business and Big Government find themselves with the same owners.

Speaking to business students in South Africa in 1976, Friedman made clear the distinction between being “pro-free enterprise and pro-business. ” It was a point he would sharpen in interviews over the following years, before remarking in 1980 that “I’m opposed to big business and I’m opposed to big government and I do believe they are in bed with one another.” Today’s Republicans seem to have forgotten Friedman’s lesson in the market-distorting and economy-threatening effects of business-government collusion.

But Trump’s ownership stakes in private companies pose a deeper harm than the government picking winners and losers (though there’s no doubt that competitors to Trump’s favored AI players will find it awfully hard to compete). Those in doubt need look no further than Trunp’s recent glowing promotion of Scotts Miracle-Gro — a major Trump donor — which led to a 6 percent jump in the company’s share price.

But America’s pitchman-in-chief doesn’t need to take official ownership stakes in companies in order to tilt the scales in their favor. Investing in them as a private citizen is often enough. As CNN reports, Trump has a strong tendency to publicly praise and promote companies in which he recently purchased stock, including 20 companies the president talked up on his Truth Social platform just days after investing in them. Trump’s stock trading is so frequent, in fact, that it amounted to more than 800 pages of his most recent 927-page financial disclosure.

Offering free White House advertising for his personal stock portfolio is bad enough; using taxpayer money to take ownership stakes in critical American industries creates opportunities for corruption on an entirely different — and more dangerous — level. Trump claims his ownership stakes are designed to ensure semiconductor companies and tech firms are serving America’s strategic interests, but he also has the bad habit of equating America’s interests with his own desire to be seen as a Xi Jinping-style strongman exerting his personal influence on powerful businessmen.

“When you combine capitalists and ownership of property with political power you have too much power concentrated,” Friedman said. “If you have free enterprise, if you have competition, then one power is offset against the other power.”

Friedman’s warning is made flesh in tech titans like Palantir’s Alex Karp and Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, who are eager to sacrifice competition for access to lucrative government deals and Trump’s personal favor. As Trump’s view of the public interest increasingly aligns with Silicon Valley’s view of its own interests, it’s worth asking if the government is even capable of serving as a watchdog for the industries it now considers friends and strategic partners.

There’s no denying Silicon Valley’s willingness to bend the knee to Trump’s demands has generated a lucrative return on executives’ personal investments. Administration officials and C-suite leaders alike have profited to the tune of billions of dollars over the past year, with Trump alone raking in more than $7 billion in cryptocurrency gains . It’s no coincidence that many of Trump’s favored tech leaders also hold significant amounts of his cryptocurrencies.

Trump’s use of state capitalism has forced a serious discussion about what kind of economy the U.S. has become, and whether the government should be in the business of favoring our corporate tech giants. Friedman would abhor Trump’s actions. Democrats must harness their new and unlikely ally to help remind Americans that free and fair competition enriches all of us, while government collusion only profits the favored few.

Max Burns is a veteran Democratic strategist and founder of Third Degree Strategies.

articles.title: Biden mourns Dolly Parton: ‘An American original’
articles.summary: Former President Biden is joining every other living commander in chief in remembering Dolly Parton, calling the country music icon “an American original.” Parton died at 80 on Tuesday in Nashville following a “brief battle with cancer,” according to her representatives. Referring to Parton as “an inspiration to millions,” Biden — who announced last year that he had…
articles.body:
Former President Biden is joining every other living commander in chief in remembering Dolly Parton, calling the country music icon “an American original.”

Parton died at 80 on Tuesday in Nashville following a “brief battle with cancer,” according to her representatives.

Referring to Parton as “an inspiration to millions,” Biden — who announced last year that he had been diagnosed with an aggressive form of prostate cancer — said in a late Tuesday social media post that the “Jolene” singer and philanthropist was “a relentless advocate for women and for equality.”

“Through her Imagination Library, she placed the gift of reading into the hands of millions of children because she understood literacy is the foundation of opportunity,” Biden said of Parton, who launched her nationwide literacy program in 1995.

“But perhaps most importantly, Dolly treated everyone with kindness and respect. She lived her values with a flair and vitality for life that was uniquely her own,” the 83-year-old former president said.

“She was a trailblazer in every sense of the word, and she will be missed by millions around the world,” Biden said.

“Jill and I are keeping her family, her friends, and her millions of fans in our prayers. God bless Dolly Parton,” he said.

Parton said in a 2021 interview that she repeatedly declined the Presidential Medal of Freedom due to personal reasons after it was offered to her during both the Biden and Trump administrations.

All four of the living former American presidents paid tribute to Parton following her death. President Trump ordered all American flags on Tuesday to be flown at half-staff in memory of the late music legend.

articles.title: Democrats favored on cost of living in new survey
articles.summary: Registered voters prefer Democrats’ approach to tackling the cost of living over Republican plans as the issue remains a top concern ahead of the November midterms, according to a new survey. The latest poll rom Reuters/Ipsos shows that 36 percent of respondents prefer the Democratic way, while 28 percent said they would prefer the GOP’s…
articles.body:
Registered voters prefer Democrats’ approach to tackling the cost of living over Republican plans as the issue remains a top concern ahead of the November midterms, according to a new survey.

The latest poll rom Reuters/Ipsos shows that 36 percent of respondents prefer the Democratic way, while 28 percent said they would prefer the GOP’s approach. The remainder said they were unsure or did not support either plan.

The statistic marks the largest advantage Democrats have had since the pollster started asking respondents the question last October — steadily growing close to one year later and amid rising costs as a result of inflation and the Iran war’s impact on energy prices.

Most American adults also disapprove of President Trump’s approach to the cost of living, with 70 percent saying as much. Roughly 21 percent said the opposite, the survey found.

The overwhelming majority of Democrats in the poll disapprove, at 93 percent while only 3 percent said they supported Trump’s approach. Independents follow with about 75 percent disapproving his handling of the issue compared to only 12 percent who favor it.

Most Republicans support Trump’s approach, though a large chunk of GOP respondents also disapprove, with 52 percent to 39 percent, respectively.

But on the economy, Democrats and Republicans are roughly tied in who has the better approach, at 35 percent to 33 percent, the numbers show.

Democrats surpassed Republicans on the issue in a separate poll from Reuters/Ipsos earlier this month , after the GOP was perceived as having the better economic agenda since at least January 2025, when Trump returned to the White House.

Similar results were seen in a recent Economist/YouGov poll , where 39 percent of respondents said they believe Democrats do “a better job handling” the economy compared to 32 percent who said the same of Republicans.

Democratic candidates have made affordability a central plank of their campaigns since it proved to be a key issue going into the 2025 elections. Republicans have also made attempts to focus on cost-of-living concerns, though Trump attempted to dismiss it late last year and into 2026 by calling the issue a hoax perpetuated by Democrats.

In February, he claimed to have “ won affordability ” and inflation during a speech at a Georgia rally, adding that he “inherited a mess.”

The annual inflation rate declined slightly to 3.4 percent in July, which remains above the Federal Reserve’s targeted 2 percent, after it reached 3.5 percent in June.

The Reuters/Ipsos survey was conducted Aug. 21-24 and included 1,215 respondents, including 951 registered voters. The margin of error is 3 percentage points.

articles.title: Trump, Vance to keynote GOP midterm convention
articles.summary: President Trump and Vice President JD Vance will address Republicans at the party’s midterm convention next month in Dallas in an effort to galvanize their MAGA base ahead of midterm elections where the House and Senate majorities are in play. Trump will appear for both nights of the gathering on September 9th and 10th, and…
articles.body:
President Trump and Vice President JD Vance will address Republicans at the party’s midterm convention next month in Dallas in an effort to galvanize their MAGA base ahead of midterm elections where the House and Senate majorities are in play.

Trump will appear for both nights of the gathering on September 9th and 10th, and deliver remarks on the final night. Vance will address attendees on the first night of the convention.

According to guidance released by the Republican National Committee, both nights of the convention will feature a total of 109 items and speakers.

Republicans are slated to cover a number of issues during the two-night event, including addressing what the party notes are the benefits of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, the Trump administration’s efforts to combat fraud, health care affordability, immigration, trade, and cultural issues.

“President Donald Trump and Republicans have delivered historic results for the American people, and every hour of this historic convention will tell that story,” RNC Chairman Joe Gruters said in a statement.

“Over two action-packed days, we will take Americans through the defining issues of our Party’s agenda and what is at stake in November. Each hour will have its own theme, its own message, and its own voices, building toward President Donald Trump’s vision for the next chapter of American greatness. This will be unlike any political convention America has seen before,” he continued.

The convention comes as Trump’s approval ratings decline, potentially having a negative effect on Republicans running in the midterms.

A Reuters/Ipsos poll released earlier this month showed Trump’s approval rating at 33 percent nationally. The Decision Desk polling average shows Democrats leading Republicans by six points on the generic ballot.
